strengths: The core idea—replacing explicit degradation labels/text prompts with continuously computed, physically interpretable spatial–spectral metrics (HFER, STU, SCM, etc.) as gating prompts—is well motivated and addressed a genuine limitation of prior prompt-based HSI restoration methods (PromptHSI, MP-HSIR).

The metric selection is not arbitrary: the paper provides a systematic pipeline (25 candidates → interpretability/coverage/discriminability criteria → Random Forest feature importance) with supporting evidence (t-SNE separation, confusion matrix in Fig. 2).

Comprehensive evaluation: 8 datasets spanning natural-scene and remote-sensing HSIs, 5 unified restoration tasks, 5 all-in-one baselines and 12 task-specific baselines, plus zero-shot evaluation on unseen degradations (motion deblurring, Poisson noise) with clear gains (e.g., +2.10dB over the best baseline for Poisson denoising).

Thorough ablations covering DP/SSAM contributions (Table 4), routing strategy comparison (Table 5), plug-and-play integration of DP into MoCE-IR and MP-HSIR (Table 6), efficiency (Table 7), and expert count/activation studies, including multi-task vs. single-task training comparisons in the supplement.
Good efficiency profile: DAMP achieves SOTA quality with the second-lowest FLOPs and inference time among unified methods, and DP adds negligible overhead.
Reproducibility is supported by a stated public code release, detailed degradation configurations, and dataset descriptions in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The headline claim of handling 'diverse, mixed, or unseen degradations' is not fully substantiated: all quantitative experiments (Tables 2 and 3) use a single degradation type per input. No experiments on mixed or spatially varying degradations are reported, despite this being the central motivation. Similarly, the global image-level metrics may not capture localized or heterogeneous degradations.

Novelty is incremental: the overall recipe (MoE with a degradation-aware router for unified restoration) closely follows MoCE-IR [54], and the main contribution reduces to swapping frequency-based routing for handcrafted metric-based routing. The SSAM (learnable scalar weighting of spatial/spectral branches) is a relatively simple design. The strong claim of 'eliminating degradation priors' is partially undermined because the six metrics are themselves handcrafted degradation descriptors selected with prior knowledge of the degradation types used in training.

The magnitude of some reported gains raises questions: e.g., +4.20dB from adding DP alone in Table 4, +5.77dB over MoCE-IR for band completion, and +2.24dB for super-resolution on ARAD are unusually large for a routing/prompting change; the paper does not explain why DP-based routing yields such outsized improvements, and no variance or multiple-seed results are provided in the main tables.

Several comparability and consistency concerns: baselines were presumably retrained/retuned under potentially different settings without clarification; some table entries look anomalous (e.g., MoCE-IR 44.17/0.924 on HyRank super-resolution vs. ~0.98 SSIM for other methods); Fig. 1 describes the CAVE capture system in a way that appears inconsistent with the cited source (GAP camera of Yasuma et al.).
Only PSNR/SSIM are reported; given the emphasis on spectral fidelity, spectral-angle or per-band error analyses are limited to small qualitative figures (Fig. 5, 6) rather than quantitative metrics.

Presentation issues: duplicated sentences in the Efficiency Analysis paragraph, some grammatical errors, and an MP-HSIR venue listed inconsistently (ICCV2025 in Fig. 1 vs. arXiv preprint in references).
No discussion of failure cases or limitations (e.g., sensitivity of metrics to scene content vs. degradation, behavior under real sensor degradations rather than synthetic ones).

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: replacing explicit degradation-type labels/text prompts with continuously computed, physically interpretable spatial–spectral degradation metrics (DP) is a sensible direction for label-free unified HSI restoration, and the metric selection pipeline (25 candidates -> interpretability/coverage/discriminability filters -> 6 metrics, documented in supplementary Sec. A) is transparent.

The evaluation is broad in scope: five known degradation tasks across eight datasets (natural and remote sensing), zero-shot evaluation on unseen degradations (motion deblurring, Poisson denoising on CAVE), plus ablations on components, routing strategy, number of experts, and single- vs. multi-task training (supplementary E).
Useful plug-and-play evidence: DP improves both MoCE-IR (+1.00 dB) and MP-HSIR (+1.99 dB) when used as a routing signal (Table 6), suggesting the contribution is more than an architecture tweak.
Efficiency analysis (Table 7) shows DP adds negligible FLOPs/parameters/latency, and the model is far cheaper than MP-HSIR or DFPIR.
The supplementary material provides dataset, degradation, and architecture details that materially aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparisons is questionable. Some reported baseline numbers look implausible or misconfigured (e.g., InstructIR at 21.91/22.05 dB on inpainting while other all-in-one methods reach 26-29 dB; MoCE-IR at 44.17/0.924 on HyRank super-resolution vs. ~48-49 for every other method). Several baselines are RGB-oriented and may not have been properly adapted to HSI, which inflates the apparent margin. The 4.20 dB jump from adding DP in the ablation (Table 4) is also suspiciously large and suggests the DP-free baseline was handicapped.

Novelty is moderate. Blind/no-reference degradation estimation is a classical topic, and metric-based routing echoes degradation-estimation-conditioned and MoE-restoration designs (e.g., MoCE-IR's frequency-based routing). The paper does not compare against or discuss blind degradation estimation approaches, which is the most natural alternative baseline for a 'label-free' framework.
The code availability statement in the abstract is an empty link ('Code is publicly available at'), undermining the reproducibility claim at submission time.

Only PSNR/SSIM are used. For hyperspectral restoration, spectral fidelity metrics (SAM, ERGAS, or per-band analysis beyond Fig. 6's qualitative curves) are standard and their absence weakens claims about preserving 'intrinsic spectral characteristics.'

Metric analysis overstates its conclusions: the confusion matrix in Fig. 2(b) shows non-trivial confusion between regions-missing and low-resolution, yet the text claims 'nearly all degradation types are correctly identified.' Additionally, the metrics are validated only on ARAD patches with synthetic degradations, leaving robustness on real degradations unverified despite motivation centered on real-world mixed degradations.

The claimed 'unified' framework is actually split: separate models for natural vs. remote sensing domains, and the headline zero-shot gains (e.g., +2.10 dB Poisson) are on CAVE, which is very close in domain (31 bands, indoor scenes) to the training data. Generalization claims would be stronger with a more distant test domain.

No limitations or ethics/broader-impact discussion; minor presentation defects (duplicated references [16]/[17], grammar slips such as 'often impractical to obtain', 'outperforming') suggest insufficient polish.

strengths: The core idea of replacing explicit degradation labels/text prompts with continuously quantified, physically interpretable spatial-spectral metrics (HFER, STU, SCM) as degradation prompts is well motivated and reasonably novel for HSI restoration, addressing a genuine practical limitation of prior prompt-based unified methods (PromptIR, MP-HSIR, MoCE-IR).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five degradation tasks across eight datasets (natural and remote sensing), comparisons against 5 unified and 12 task-specific baselines, zero-shot generalization to two unseen degradations, efficiency analysis (Table 7), and plug-and-play experiments showing DP improves MoCE-IR and MP-HSIR (Table 6).

Thoughtful supporting analyses: metric selection pipeline with interpretability/coverage/discriminability criteria and Random Forest importance (supplementary Sec. A, Fig. 7), t-SNE/confusion-matrix evidence that metrics separate degradation types (Fig. 2b), ablations on key components (Table 4), routing strategies (Table 5), number of total/activated experts (Tables 11-12), and single- vs multi-task training (Table 10).
Good efficiency profile: DP adds negligible FLOPs/parameters/latency, and the full model is competitive with or faster than prior unified methods.
Reproducibility support is decent: code is stated to be publicly available, and the supplementary material details datasets, degradation configurations, and architecture.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling 'mixed' degradations (abstract, contributions, Section 3.1) is not directly supported by the experiments: all main evaluations (Table 2) and the zero-shot tests (Table 3) use single degradation types. No experiment composes multiple degradations (e.g., blur + noise + band missing) or evaluates real-world degraded HSIs, so the motivating claim about complex real-world mixtures remains unverified.

Metric-based degradation estimation is potentially circular and content-dependent: HFER, STU, and SCM are computed from the degraded image and conflate scene content with degradation (e.g., a naturally smooth scene resembles a blurred one). The metric analysis (Fig. 2) is built on synthetic degradations of ARAD patches only, so robustness of the DP representation to scene variation, sensor differences, and real degradations is unproven.

The metric selection pipeline is trained on five synthetic degradation types from a single dataset (ARAD), raising concerns that the chosen metric set and the DP embedding are dataset- and degradation-family-specific; no cross-dataset validation of the metric selection is provided.

Evaluation relies solely on PSNR/SSIM despite the paper's emphasis on spectral fidelity; standard hyperspectral metrics such as SAM or ERGAS are absent, weakening the claim that SSAM 'better preserves the intrinsic spectral characteristics' (Fig. 6 is only a qualitative per-band error plot).

Naming inconsistency: STU is defined in Table 1 as measuring spectral smoothness ('spatial texture uniformity' with a spectral geometric-to-arithmetic mean formula), while Fig. 2(c) presents it as a spatial discriminator separating blur from missing regions; the physical interpretation vs. usage is inconsistent and confusing.

The 'unified' claim is softened by training separate models for natural-scene and remote-sensing domains (Section 4.1), and the zero-shot generality test is narrow: only two unseen degradations on CAVE, with a fixed 15-pixel, 45-degree motion blur kernel and one Poisson scaling factor.

Methodological novelty is incremental at the architecture level: the framework largely recombines a Swin-style U-Net, MoE routing (close to MoCE-IR), and prompt conditioning; the main novelty lies in the metric prompts, whose theoretical grounding is limited to heuristic selection criteria.
No explicit limitations discussion appears in the main paper (the supplementary promises a limitations section, but its content is not evident from the provided material).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: unified training across five HSI restoration tasks on eight datasets (natural and remote sensing), plus zero-shot evaluation on unseen degradations (motion deblurring, Poisson noise), comparisons against 17 baselines including task-specific, unified, unsupervised/self-supervised, and real-world data (Table 20).

The core idea—replacing black-box prompt embeddings with interpretable spatial-spectral metrics as conditioning/router signals—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly distinct from prior prompt-based HSI restoration (PromptHSI, MP-HSIR), which rely on external degradation labels.

Extensive and largely convincing ablations: routing strategy comparison (Table 5), leave-one-out metric ablation (Table 17), expert count/top-k ablations, routing noise sensitivity, and expert activation heatmaps (Fig. 12) that directly substantiate the claimed spatial/spectral expert specialization and load balancing.

Thorough supplementary material covering metric selection pipeline, degradation configurations, architecture details, scalability with spectral band count, and mixed/localized degradation stress tests (Table 13, 14).
Honest limitations section acknowledging unvalidated real-world degradation diversity and the need for separate domain-specific training, plus an impact statement.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis—that interpretability of the DP representation is what drives better generalization—is supported only indirectly (Tables 3 and 5). The paper asserts that black-box prompts project unseen degradations onto learned manifolds while DP remains faithful, but does not provide a direct analysis (e.g., DP values on unseen degradations, failure cases where metrics are misleading) to establish the causal mechanism; the same gains could stem from the stronger signal content of the metrics rather than interpretability per se.

The methodological contribution is relatively incremental: a U-shaped restoration backbone with a MoE whose router is conditioned on six hand-crafted image statistics plus fixed expert branches with learnable spatial/spectral fusion scalars. Much of the gain likely comes from well-executed engineering and conditioning rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Some reported gaps strain credulity and merit clarification: e.g., the routing ablation (Table 5) shows a >4.6dB gap over implicit-prompt routing, and DP alone yields a 4.20dB jump over the baseline (Table 4)—unusually large for a conditioning change; no variance/seeds are reported anywhere, and 'randomly evaluate each degradation type across three datasets' leaves the selection protocol ambiguous.

The claim of 'universal' degradation representation is weakened by the dependence on metrics calibrated to the training degradation set; the limitations section concedes rare or physically distinct degradations may need additional metrics, but the paper does not test how DP behaves under distributional shift of the metrics themselves (beyond the two unseen types).

Reproducibility concerns: the abstract and supplementary reference a public GitHub repository, but the link is missing/blank in the manuscript; several visual analyses (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) are qualitative only, and some appendix claims (E.5 fine-tuning results, E.6 comparisons) are described in text with limited detail (Table 16 protocol unclear).

Specialized scope: results are HSI-specific and the learned components (SSAM branches) are simple; generalization of the prompting idea beyond HSI is not explored, limiting significance for the broader ICML community.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (unified HSI restoration) and proposes a clean, interpretable alternative to explicit degradation labels and opaque latent prompts: a 6-dimensional degradation prompt computed directly from the degraded input, used to route a Mixture-of-Experts.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: eight datasets spanning natural and remote-sensing HSI, five degradation tasks, zero-shot evaluation on unseen degradations (motion blur, Poisson noise), comparisons against 5 unified and 12 task-specific baselines, plus unsupervised/self-supervised and fully-supervised task-specific SOTAs, and a real-world dataset experiment.

The appendix contains substantial supporting analysis: metric-selection pipeline, leave-one-out metric ablations, expert-count ablations, routing noise sensitivity, expert activation heatmaps supporting the claimed spatial/spectral specialization, and computational scalability across spectral band counts.
Efficiency results are convincing: DAMP uses fewer FLOPs than most all-in-one baselines, and the overhead of metric extraction and routing is negligible (<0.2ms).
The limitations section is honest and specific (unvalidated rare/real-world degradations, per-domain training requirement), and the paper appropriately discusses rather than hides these constraints.
weaknesses: Some reported numbers are implausibly large and need stronger justification. The routing-strategy ablation (Table 5) shows the DP router beating frequency-based routing by 3.71 dB and degradation-type routing by 5.16 dB on the same backbone; gains of this magnitude from a 6-dimensional condition vector alone (baseline 45.82 dB -> 50.02 dB with DP) suggest either a strong task-identity leak via the metrics or potentially under-trained/misconfigured ablation baselines. The paper should clarify whether all routing variants received identical training budgets and hyperparameter tuning.

The central scientific claim - that interpretability of the metrics is what 'fundamentally enhances generalization' to unseen degradations - is asserted rather than causally demonstrated. The evidence shows that DP is a good conditioning signal; it does not isolate interpretability as the mechanism. A control experiment with an equally expressive but non-interpretable learned scalar/statistical embedding of matched dimensionality would be needed to support this claim.

Novelty is moderate. Each component (handcrafted quality metrics, learned conditioning, top-k MoE with noisy routing, spatial/spectral dual-branch attention with learnable fusion weights) is standard; the contribution is primarily their combination and application to HSI. The 'Spatial Experts' vs 'Spectral Experts' polarization is an emergent behavior presented as a design, and the learnable-vs-instance-specific lambda choice is not ablated.

Zero-shot comparisons have fairness concerns. The baselines (PromptIR, InstructIR, DFPIR, MoCE-IR) are RGB-oriented unified models applied to HSI; their weak zero-shot numbers (e.g., MP-HSIR at 23.63 dB on motion deblurring vs 30.53 dB for PromptIR) are not fully explained. Additionally, the fixed zero-shot degradation settings (45-degree motion kernel radius 15, fixed Poisson scaling) may inadvertently favor methods whose metrics align with those specific statistics.

Gains over the strongest baselines on several tasks are marginal (e.g., inpainting on PaviaC: 29.41 vs 29.29; band completion on Xiong'an: 56.61 vs 56.55), so the SOTA claim rests heavily on a few large per-task gains whose robustness (variance across seeds) is not reported anywhere in the paper.

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract and supplementary reference a GitHub repository but the URL is empty in the manuscript; no error bars or multiple seeds are reported; the exact protocol for retraining baselines under the unified HSI setting (where many baselines are RGB methods) is only briefly described.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing explicit degradation priors and opaque black-box prompt embeddings with an interpretable 6-dimensional spatial-spectral Degradation Prompt (DP) is a genuine and sensible contribution for HSI restoration, where spectral fidelity matters and priors are hard to specify.

The DP design is empirically grounded rather than ad hoc: a systematic selection pipeline (25 candidate metrics → interpretability/coverage filtering → Random Forest feature importance) is documented in the supplementary, with t-SNE clustering, confusion matrices, and correlation analyses (Fig. 2, Fig. 7) supporting that the metrics discriminate degradation types and track severity.

Comprehensive evaluation: eight datasets spanning natural and remote sensing domains, five unified training tasks, two zero-shot unseen degradation tasks, comparisons against 5 unified and 12 task-specific baselines, plus real-world data evaluation (Table 20) and comparisons with unsupervised/self-supervised methods (Table 16).

Extensive ablations strengthen the claims: component ablation (Table 4), routing-strategy comparison against frequency-based, degradation-type, and implicit-prompt routing (Table 5), leave-one-out metric analysis (Table 17), expert-count studies (Tables 10-11), routing noise sensitivity (Table 12), and expert activation heatmaps confirming spatial/spectral specialization (Fig. 12).

Efficiency is credibly addressed: DAMP uses fewer FLOPs (313.8G) and less latency (133ms) than PromptIR, DFPIR, and MP-HSIR, and DP overhead is negligible (<0.2ms); scalability to 256-512 spectral bands is also analyzed (Table 19).
Honest and specific limitations discussion (unvalidated rare/real-world degradations, per-domain training requirement) paired with concrete future work; impact statement present.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that 'interpretability fundamentally enhances generalization' is argued mostly narratively; the zero-shot gains could partly stem from the metric features being robust rather than from interpretability per se. A controlled experiment isolating interpretable-vs-black-box prompt representations under matched capacity exists (Table 5) but only on known degradations.

The magnitude of gains warrants scrutiny: +5.61dB over the no-DP/no-SSAM baseline (Table 4) and large margins over all unified baselines suggest the baseline may be under-tuned; a stronger, better-optimized ablation baseline would make the component contributions more convincing.

DP metrics are computed from global statistics of the input, which risks conflating image content with degradation (e.g., smooth natural scenes vs. textured remote sensing scenes yield different HFER/SCM even at identical degradation). The spatially heterogeneous analysis (Table 13, E.3) partially mitigates this, but content-degradation confounding across domains is not directly tested, despite the model still requiring separate training per domain.

The routing function concatenates GAP features with the DP vector (Eq. 3), so the effective role of the DP versus generic pooled features is somewhat entangled; the routing-strategy ablation helps, but a variant routing purely on DP would clarify the mechanism.

Novelty is moderate at the component level: the backbone is a fairly standard Swin-style U-shaped network, SSAM is a lightweight two-branch attention block, and MoE routing is well-established; the main originality lies in the interpretable metric prompting formulation and its empirical support rather than new architectural machinery.

Several comparisons (e.g., InstructIR, PromptIR on HSI tasks) involve RGB-oriented methods retrained under the MP-HSIR protocol; fairness is plausible but per-method adaptation details are not fully described in the main text.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL is left blank in the abstract and Section C, which weakens the reproducibility claim; a few grammatical errors (e.g., 'often impractical to obtain', 'such as denoising ... and') and the very high reported PSNR values for band completion (63.49dB) merit a sanity-check note since most bands are observed.
